graphicEarnsIt.says: A sheet of alphabet specimens, each letter set in a different found face, acting as the stock the headline is cut from. Between the two beats the cells for A, M, N, O, R, S empty out and the words RANSOM NOTES appear above, so the picture encodes a one-to-one accounting: these six letters were removed from the supply and are now in the title. It shows the making of the word, which the word alone cannot show, and it is the one object that survives the cut and changes across it.

A sheet of alphabet specimens, each cell a differently cut letter, is the stock the title is torn from. Between beat 1 and beat 2 the cells holding A, M, N, O, R and S empty out, and those are exactly the distinct letters of RANSOM standing above. The picture shows a supply being consumed: which letters were taken, from where, and that the wordmark is assembled rather than typed. LEFT has no picture at all, only type on a flat field.

A grid of every available letter, an alphabet specimen sheet, used as a source inventory. Between the two beats the exact letters spelling the title are physically removed from it: the A, M, N, O, R and S slots go blank while every other cell stays intact. The picture encodes supply and depletion, the wordmark was cut out of this sheet, and the count of missing cells matches the letters in the name. It also gives the film one object that survives the cut and changes across it. Small flaw: beat 1 boxes only four of the six letters it later removes, so the promise does not tally exactly with the payoff. LEFT has no picture at all, only type.

perBeat.why: LEFT is one word floating in an otherwise empty frame, while RIGHT pairs the same word with a found-type specimen tray that fills the lower third and flags the letters about to be taken.
RIGHT's tray now has holes exactly where A, M, N, O, R, S used to sit, so the frame proves where the headline's letters came from; LEFT just enlarges the lockup and says nothing new.
